title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
constraints: s consists of ASCII characters, no special cases

examples.explanation: The longest valid substring is "abc", so the answer is 3.
The longest valid substring is "b", so the answer is 1.

hints.content: A substring is a contiguous region, and you are looking for the longest one that satisfies a condition. Which pattern handles that?
Move the right pointer forward one character at a time. When is the window invalid, and which pointer fixes it?
A window is invalid when a character occurs twice inside it. You need counts, not just a set, because you must know where the earlier occurrence is.

left = 0
for right in range(n):
    count[s[right]] += 1
    while count[s[right]] > 1:
        count[s[left]] -= 1
        left++
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
Use int[256] for ASCII counts, or a HashMap<Character, Integer>. The variant that jumps left directly to lastIndex + 1 is faster but hides the invariant.

invariant: Every character in the current window appears at most once, and left is the smallest index for which that holds.
whyThisPattern: The signal is 'contiguous substring + longest + validity'. The window grows to the right one character at a time, and only shrinks when the condition breaks, so each character enters and leaves the window once. That gives O(n) with no rescans, instead of checking every substring.
bruteForce: Start at every index and extend to the end while tracking a set: O(n^2) time. At n = 100,000 that is about 10^10 operations. A sliding window touches each character at most twice, so it is 100,000 times faster.
interviewExplanation: I maintain a sliding window from left to right together with a count of each character inside it. I extend right, and as soon as a character appears twice I move left forward until the window is valid again. Since left only ever moves forward, every character enters and leaves the window once, giving O(n) time and constant extra space for ASCII input.
commonMistakes: Checking validity before adding the current character, so the duplicate is never detected.
Shrinking the window only once when several duplicates exist at the same time.
Using a set instead of counts, which tells you the character repeats but not where the previous copy is.

breakdown.explanation: A single string. Nothing needs matching against anything else, which rules out the compare-two-inputs family of problems.

options: The length of the longest substring without repeats
The count of distinct characters in the string
breakdown.explanation: A length, and only over contiguous runs. A subsequence would be a different problem with a very different feel, so the word 'substring' is load-bearing.

breakdown.prompt: Why does a window work instead of checking every substring?
options: Once a repeat appears, the answer's best start is the position after the previous copy
Every substring has a unique set of characters
Windows can be checked in constant time each
breakdown.explanation: A repeat makes any window starting before the earlier copy invalid, so the earliest valid start jumps forward to just past it. That lets a single window sweep left to right without ever moving backwards.
